registerContract.formal: course convention for formal you turns: no contractions, no gonna/wanna/kinda/gotta, full modal forms (I would, I will), formal lexis where a plain-register word competes (purchase/buy allowed either way, but no slang); sentence-final prepositions are native in every register and are never flagged; fronted forms (to whom, in which) are a taught option in L8-type lessons, not a rule
registerContract.neutral: contractions allowed (I'd, that's, doesn't), everyday lexis, no slang list items
registerContract.informal: contractions expected, phrasal verbs welcome (sort out, put off, go for), interjection openers allowed (Honestly, Look), slang list still limited to the approved informal set (kind of, a bit, no way)
registerContract.stability: all three you registers identical within every P1/P2 episode (registerPlan.mode constant); shift mode and relay reserved for later paths
registerContract.themTurns: interlocutor register follows the register chosen for the episode (in this course formal-role them turns use full forms and friend/neighbor them turns contract) so the learner hears the target register before producing it; this is an instructional choice, not a claim about how real speakers in those roles talk
registerContract.grammarNote: English marks register by contraction, modal choice and lexis, not by pronoun; registerPlan.registers carries the three string values above in place of Sie/du, field shape unchanged

genderSafety.speakerGender: neutral on all twenty lessons; no alternates objects anywhere in P1/P2
genderSafety.rule: learner turns never contain gender-marked self-reference; them turns may address the learner only with you; gendered role nouns (chairman, waitress, policeman, spokesman) are banned in all turns and replaced by chair, server, officer, spokesperson; detector emits a warning, not an error, because some surface forms (host, actor) are neutral in US usage
genderSafety.canonicalGender: omitted on every lesson (only required when marked)

orthography.spelling: US canonical (favor, center, organize, traveling, check, program, license); UK forms in canonical text are warnings; where a blank or recall answer has a UK spelling the author lists it explicitly in acceptedAnswers; nothing is expanded automatically
orthography.apostrophe: U+2019 canonical in every targetText and chunk; apostrophe unification of learner input (U+0027, U+02BC) is a planned runtime-integration item, not present today, so authors list the U+0027 form of any answer containing an apostrophe in acceptedAnswers; validator rewrites nothing
orthography.numbers: always words in voiced text (two hundred dollars, thirty percent, three days); digits are errors in any targetText, chunk, blank answer or example
orthography.dashes: no em dashes in canonical text; use a comma, semicolon or colon so chunk boundaries stay inside the token rule
orthography.titles: no periods after Mr/Ms in canonical text to avoid TTS pauses; prefer first names or roles

segmentation.unit: token = maximal run of letters and digits with internal apostrophes or hyphens; the space U+0020 is the joiner
segmentation.contractions: one token (I’d, don’t, that’s, we’ll); the apostrophe never opens a boundary
segmentation.hyphens: one token (trade-off, long-term, self-paced, on-site, part-time); a hyphenated trophy is therefore a legal single-token lemma
segmentation.punctuation: attached to the chunk it ends (whereas,); commas inside a chunk are allowed only when the chunk still has 1–4 tokens
segmentation.lengths: them 6–20, you1 14–26, build focus span 7–12, you2 12–24, you3 10–22; scale 1, no rounding

acceptedInput.normalization: planned (runtime integration, not yet implemented): NFC, trim, collapse spaces, lowercase (en-US), strip terminal . ! ? , ;, unify apostrophes, then compare; until it ships, drafts rely only on the explicit acceptedAnswers list and the existing comparison
acceptedInput.variants: nothing is auto-added; the author writes every accepted variant explicitly (draft acceptedAnswers: US form, UK form where one exists, U+0027 apostrophe form); plural/possessive variants are listed only when they are correct in the frame; the new English gate checks list structure, correctness stays with semantic review
acceptedInput.registerBearing: a contracted and an uncontracted form are never mutually accepted unless both are listed explicitly, because the contraction carries the register the blank is testing
acceptedInput.chips: visible chips must be semantically distinct after normalization; two chips that differ only by punctuation are a validator error (B2-EN-CHIP-DUP)

productive: the compromise I would recommend is

lessons.scene: viewing a pricier downtown apartment; the leasing agent compares it with a cheaper one in the suburbs
lessons.openingMove: compare: on the one hand downtown costs far more, on the other the suburb means an hour on the train each way
lessons.challenge: objection: are two hours a day really worth three hundred dollars a month?
lessons.answerMove: concede: granted, the premium is steep, but the main advantage is that evenings stay free, and that matters far more than the number
lessons.steer: bottom line: sign today or keep looking?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: on balance the trade-off favors time, so I will take the downtown unit
lessons.requiredCarrier: on the one hand … on the other; granted; on balance

lessons.scene: a colleague wants to carpool; you prefer the train for the daily commute
lessons.openingMove: position: the train suits me, since I can work on the way, whereas the main drawback of driving is parking
lessons.challenge: counter-example: the trains were canceled twice last week
lessons.answerMove: rebut: that’s true, but one bad week doesn’t change the pattern; I lose twenty minutes a day hunting for a space, which means driving costs more time, not less
lessons.steer: edge case: what if the company paid for parking?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: even so, the train wins, as a result of the working time it gives back
lessons.requiredCarrier: since; which means that; as a result; that’s true, but

lessons.scene: your manager reviews a request to work from home three days a week
lessons.openingMove: position: I would argue that remote days produce more focused work, even though they cost some visibility
lessons.challenge: objection: team cohesion suffers when half the team is at home
lessons.answerMove: concede: admittedly, cohesion needs face time; that said, a fixed overlap day solves most of it
lessons.steer: final condition: a minimum of three office days, non-negotiable?
lessons.closingMove: counteroffer: two fixed office days with a shared core window, reviewed after a quarter
lessons.requiredCarrier: although/even though; admittedly; that said; I would argue

lessons.scene: at an equipment rental desk you decide whether to rent or buy a projector for a six-month project
lessons.openingMove: reason: after six months of rental we’ll have paid the purchase price, so buying looks smarter
lessons.challenge: constraint: the model is updated every year; if you had bought last year you’d be stuck with the old one now
lessons.answerMove: rebut: even if that were true, a one-year-old model would still do the job; otherwise we’d be renting forever
lessons.steer: edge case: what if the project ends after three months?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: in case it ends early we might well resell it, so buying is worthwhile either way
lessons.requiredCarrier: mixed conditional; otherwise; in case; might well

lessons.scene: a friend pushes a cheap mountain week by bus; you prefer four days at the coast by plane
lessons.openingMove: compare: the mountains are cheaper, whereas the coast gives us actual rest
lessons.challenge: refusal: no way I’m paying three hundred for a flight; the bus is ten hours, but it’s nearly free
lessons.answerMove: counteroffer: I’m not prepared to spend ten hours on a bus each way; unless the Tuesday fare is gone, we fly and split the difference; failing that, a shorter coast trip
lessons.steer: final condition: a hard cap of five hundred dollars each
lessons.closingMove: conclude: I’d expect the coast to come in under that, and the rest we get outweighs the extra fare
lessons.requiredCarrier: I’d expect; I’m not prepared to; unless; failing that
recycles: on the one hand … on the other

lessons.scene: a shop owner you know asks whether to accept app payments or stay cash-only
lessons.openingMove: reason: regarding fees, the app takes two percent, whereas cash costs you counting time and bank runs
lessons.challenge: reported objection: my accountant said cash was simpler and safer
lessons.answerMove: rebut: she said it was simpler, but as for safety, a till full of cash is the bigger risk
lessons.steer: audience: half the customers are older and distrust phones
lessons.closingMove: propose: I would suggest keeping both for a year, so the convenience is there without forcing anyone
lessons.requiredCarrier: backshifted reported speech; regarding/as for; I would suggest

lessons.scene: a friend says you should drop the evening language class and just use an app
lessons.openingMove: compare: the app is cheaper and portable, whereas the class gives me real speaking practice
lessons.challenge: objection: you can speak with the app too, and nobody notices when you skip
lessons.answerMove: concede: true, but that’s exactly the point; the class gives me discipline that I don’t have alone
lessons.steer: constraint: you only have two free evenings a week
lessons.closingMove: counteroffer: what if we do the class on Tuesdays and the app the rest, so we’re agreed that neither gets dropped
lessons.requiredCarrier: what if we; so we’re agreed that (how about we and shall we appear as terms, not required)

lessons.scene: a mentor helps you weigh a startup offer against a bank offer paying thirty percent more
lessons.openingMove: position: arguably the startup, in which I’d lead a small team, offers more growth
lessons.challenge: objection: growth doesn’t pay the rent; thirty percent is a lot of growth
lessons.answerMove: rebut: by growth I mean skills I can sell later, something the bank managers, to whom I’d be one analyst in two hundred, won’t give me
lessons.steer: edge case: could you go back and negotiate?
lessons.closingMove: counteroffer: I’d go back to the startup and ask for equity, in which case the gap shrinks
lessons.requiredCarrier: in which; to whom; by X I mean (what I mean is appears as a term, not required)

lessons.scene: a neighbor hears you might move to another city for a job and tries to talk you out of it
lessons.openingMove: reason: the job is better, and since the rent there is lower I’d save, even though I’d lose the neighborhood
lessons.challenge: interruption-objection: you’d lose your whole network, and networks take years
lessons.answerMove: concede: fair point, but let me finish; to be fair, most of my network is online anyway
lessons.steer: audience: what will you tell your parents, who’ll hate it?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: nonetheless, I’ll tell them the move is the right call, and I’ll visit every month
lessons.requiredCarrier: let me finish; fair point, but; to be fair

lessons.scene: a residents’ committee must pick one parking policy: a ban, paid permits, or no change
lessons.openingMove: compare: firstly a ban is cleanest, moreover permits bring income, whereas doing nothing costs least but solves nothing
lessons.challenge: objection: permits need staff and enforcement we cannot afford
lessons.answerMove: rebut: that is true, but the fees cover the staff within a year, which a ban never does
lessons.steer: summary: give the committee one recommendation to vote on
lessons.closingMove: conclude: ultimately paid permits are the compromise I recommend, because they change behavior without a ban
lessons.requiredCarrier: firstly; moreover; ultimately

lessons.scene: your accountant asks why the supplier invoice is two hundred dollars above the quote
lessons.openingMove: explain: the difference is due to a rate change mid-month, which means the second half was billed at the new hourly rate
lessons.challenge: precision request: which line exactly, and why was the change not announced?
lessons.answerMove: clarify: what I mean is line three; the notice went to the old address, so nobody saw it
lessons.steer: bottom line: can the discrepancy be corrected, or do we pay it?
lessons.closingMove: summarize: in short, the discrepancy comes from one unannounced rate change, and I will request a credit for the notice failure
lessons.requiredCarrier: due to; which means that; what I mean is; in short

lessons.scene: a newcomer in your building asks how the recycling works here; you explain the building’s own posted bin notice (a fictional house rule, not a general law)
lessons.openingMove: explain: according to the notice in our bin room, paper goes in the blue bin so that it stays dry, plastics in the yellow one in order to keep the two streams separate
lessons.challenge: counter-example: the guy upstairs throws greasy pizza boxes in blue and nobody cares
lessons.answerMove: rebut: the hauler’s letter says grease contaminates the batch; consequently they can refuse the container and the building pays for an extra pickup
lessons.steer: edge case: and glass with a lid still on?
lessons.closingMove: summarize: to sum up, by our notice it’s lids off, grease out, and when in doubt ask the caretaker rather than guess
lessons.requiredCarrier: so that; in order to; consequently; to sum up

lessons.scene: your manager wants the causal chain behind a two-week delay before a client call
lessons.openingMove: reason: the delay stems from the vendor delivering late, which pushed testing into the holiday week, which halved our capacity
lessons.challenge: objection: that sounds like a list of excuses rather than a cause
lessons.answerMove: concede: admittedly, we underestimated testing time from the start; the vendor only made it visible
lessons.steer: audience: say it the way the client needs to hear it
lessons.closingMove: propose: I would propose that we tell the client the root cause was our estimate, and that the new date carries a buffer
lessons.requiredCarrier: stems from; admittedly; I would propose that

lessons.scene: a friend asks how the coffee chain’s points scheme actually works
lessons.openingMove: explain: points are credited the day after a purchase and can be redeemed once you hit two hundred
lessons.challenge: precision request: so how many coffees is two hundred points, and why the one-day delay?
lessons.answerMove: clarify: in other words about twenty coffees; the delay is for refund checks, so a canceled order can’t earn anything
lessons.steer: edge case: and if I don’t use them for a year?
lessons.closingMove: summarize: to sum up, earn after a day, redeem at two hundred, and expiry after twelve months of inactivity
lessons.requiredCarrier: modal passives; nominalization (expiry); in other words

lessons.scene: a neighbor asks why you left the internet provider everyone uses
lessons.openingMove: reason: the old one had three outages a month, whereas the new one, which runs on fiber, hasn’t dropped once
lessons.challenge: objection: the new one’s cheaper, so it’s probably worse
lessons.answerMove: rebut: the difference is that they own the network in which our street’s cable runs, so they pay no rental fees to the old provider; cheap isn’t the cause here
lessons.steer: final condition: but you’re locked in for two years?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: on top of that there’s no contract, so if the outages come back I just leave
lessons.requiredCarrier: in which relatives; whereas; the difference is that; on top of that

lessons.scene: a colleague got a parking fine and asks what the notice itself says about appealing; you explain the process printed on that notice (a fictional issuer, not legal advice)
lessons.openingMove: explain: the notice says you file the appeal online within its fourteen-day window, otherwise the reduced amount lapses; in case they ask for proof, keep the photos
lessons.challenge: constraint: the deadline is Friday and the portal is down
lessons.answerMove: compare: online is instant, whereas by mail the notice says they go by the postmark; provided that it’s stamped by Friday it should count, but confirm that on the number printed on the letter
lessons.steer: summary: give me the three steps in order
lessons.closingMove: summarize: firstly write the appeal, then attach the photos and send it through the portal; failing that, mail it and keep a dated receipt
lessons.requiredCarrier: otherwise; in case; provided that; failing that

lessons.scene: a friend asks why your group trip collapsed a week before departure
lessons.openingMove: reason: it failed because of one wrong assumption; we assumed everyone could pay in June, so we booked nothing refundable
lessons.challenge: counter-example: if you’d booked earlier, the prices would’ve been fine
lessons.answerMove: rebut: even if I had, two people still couldn’t pay; the assumption was that everyone had the money, and that was the problem, not the timing
lessons.steer: lesson learned: what would you do differently?
lessons.closingMove: conclude: next time we might well collect deposits first, so a dropout doesn’t sink the rest
lessons.requiredCarrier: mixed conditional; even if I had; the assumption was that; might well

lessons.scene: a clinic coordinator has explained why your specialist booking was refused and now checks that you understood the clinic’s own booking rule (a fictional clinic policy, no medical advice)
lessons.openingMove: explain: as I understand it, a specialist slot can only be booked once a referral has been entered by a general practitioner
lessons.challenge: precision request: what exactly did the receptionist tell you on the phone?
lessons.answerMove: clarify: she said that a referral was required and that mine had not arrived, so I called my doctor that afternoon; regarding the timing, she said nothing
lessons.steer: edge case: and what did you understand about urgent cases?
lessons.closingMove: summarize: as for urgent cases, you said the practitioner can flag the referral, but unless that flag is set the request waits like any other
lessons.requiredCarrier: backshifted reported speech; regarding / as for; unless

lessons.scene: at a town meeting a skeptical neighbor asks why a bike-share scheme deserves public money; you argue from the pilot’s own survey (fictional figures)
lessons.openingMove: reason: congestion costs the town more than the scheme; in the pilot survey about a third of riders said they would otherwise have driven in at eight
lessons.challenge: interruption-objection: nobody rides in winter, so it’s money for six months
lessons.answerMove: concede: fair point, but let me finish; to be fair, the car numbers drop in summer too, which is when the road is dug up
lessons.steer: bottom line: would you pay for it from your own taxes?
lessons.closingMove: propose: how about we fund a one-year pilot and tie year two to measured congestion
lessons.requiredCarrier: let me finish; fair point, but; to be fair; how about we

lessons.scene: a city official asks you to trace how the committee reached its parking decision
lessons.openingMove: explain: firstly the survey showed demand, moreover the cost model favored permits, and as a consequence the committee voted
lessons.challenge: objection: that chain skips the public consultation entirely
lessons.answerMove: clarify: by the survey I mean the consultation; four hundred responses were counted before the cost model was built
lessons.steer: summary: state the chain for the record in one sentence
lessons.closingMove: conclude: ultimately, for the record, the decision followed from the consultation, the cost model and the vote, in that order
lessons.requiredCarrier: firstly; moreover; ultimately; as a consequence; for the record

trophyLedger.forbiddenCheck: all twenty lemmas and all twenty familyKeys checked case-folded against the 471-entry forbidden A1/A2/reservedB1 list supplied in the prerequisites: zero exact hits, zero inflectional hits (no plural, past or comparative of a forbidden lemma), twenty distinct families within P1/P2; every lemma is one token (hyphen internal), none is a function word, auxiliary, phrasal verb or proper noun; six stance/argument items (admittedly, arguably, nonetheless, consequently, ultimately, trade-off) meet the rail’s aim list; semantic near-family review remains open per nearFamilyDecisions

nearFamilyDecisions.decision: allowed: opaque compound, adjective family worthwhile ≠ connector while; not a derivation
allowed: different lexeme and different sense (final judgment versus temporal); not a synonym swap because the B1 lemma is temporal
allowed: Latin differ- family versus discrep-; no shared stem in English
allowed: distinct family and sense (ease of transaction versus physical comfort)
familyKey underestimate kept separate from estimate deliberately; a later estimate trophy would be a near-family error and is reserved against
familyKey weigh; weight and weigh are reserved against for later paths
noun pos declared; the verb sense appears in the same lesson and is accepted as the same family, so no second appeal trophy may exist
compound family drawback, independent of draw/back; disadvantage reserved as a term, never a trophy, to avoid the inflated-B1 synonym trap
hyphenated single token per rail; validator must treat U+002D as token-internal; non-hyphenated tradeoff is accepted input only

mechanicalValidationRules: B2-EN-01 contraction regex (\b\w+’(s|re|ve|ll|d|m|t)\b, n’t, let’s) in any you turn whose register is formal → error; in them turns of formal interlocutors → warning
B2-EN-02 slang list (gonna, wanna, kinda, gotta, ain’t, y’all, dunno) outside register informal → error; inside informal → warning if more than one per turn
B2-EN-03 UK spelling detector (-our, -ise, -re, -ll- doubling, programme, cheque) in canonical text → warning; validator never rewrites
B2-EN-04 any digit in targetText, chunk, blank answer, recall answer, term or example → error

B2-EN-05 apostrophe: U+0027 in canonical text → warning (autofix suggested), U+2019 canonical; any answer containing U+2019 must also list its U+0027 form in acceptedAnswers → error if missing (runtime unification is a later item)

B2-EN-06 lengths by token rule: them 6–20, you1 14–26, focus span 7–12 (framePrefix+chunks+frameSuffix minus frames counted as chunk tokens), you2 12–24, you3 10–22; hyphen and apostrophe are token-internal
B2-EN-07 build: 5–8 chunks, each 1–4 tokens, no edge whitespace, reconstruction byte-equal after NFC; exactly 2 distractors; a distractor equal to a chunk after normalization → error

B2-EN-08 cloze/synthesis: 2–4 / 1–2 blanks, indices once in order, reconstruction byte-equal; choices exactly 4 distinct after normalization and apostrophe unification, exactly one accepted, at most one choices blank per cloze
B2-EN-09 recall answer 1–3 tokens, acceptedAnswers includes answer, fallbackChoices 4 distinct

B2-EN-10 trophy: lemma single token, equals ledger row by pathNumber+lessonNumber, surface is a whole token of dialogue[turnIndex], lemma and familyKey not in forbidden set and unique across the language B2 ledger

B2-EN-11 moves: you1 in path whitelist, you2 in {concede,rebut,clarify,explain,compare,counteroffer}, you3 in {conclude,propose,summarize,counteroffer,relay,request}, pairwise distinct; relay forbidden in P1/P2
B2-EN-12 registerPlan.mode constant and all three registers equal and in {formal,neutral,informal}; speakerGender neutral, no alternates, no canonicalGender
B2-EN-13 gendered role noun list (chairman, waitress, policeman, spokesman, fireman, stewardess) anywhere → warning
B2-EN-14 base objects: every base is {de:S} only; situation is {de:S,en:S}; any en key elsewhere → error
B2-EN-15 chips: two chunks identical after normalization → error B2-EN-CHIP-DUP; reorder-uniqueness is not checked mechanically and is delegated to semantic rule S4
B2-EN-16 terms 8–10, each targetText occurs folded in dialogue or a pattern example; speak 3 entries with turnIndex 1,3,5 and 2–4 distinct whole tokens of that turn
B2-EN-17 requiredCarrier of lesson n must appear verbatim (folded) in a dialogue turn, pattern example or term of lesson ≤ n before any blank or choices set of lesson n requires it
B2-EN-18 sentence-initial However count across a path > 3 → warning
semanticReviewRules: S1 argument coherence: the challenge changes something real (constraint, counter-example, refusal, precision) and the steer changes the task; you3 answers the steer, not you1
S2 B2 not inflated B1: the lesson carries reasons, implications and a qualified recommendation or a causal chain, not harder nouns in A2 frames
S3 register native: formal turns read as a careful US speaker without contractions, informal turns as a friend; no mixed register inside a you turn

S4 build order uniqueness: the canonical chunk order must be the only grammatical and plausible order given syntax and meaning, not punctuation alone; a native reviewer must try at least one alternative order
S5 also-correct check: distractors and the three wrong choices must be wrong in this frame (grammar, meaning or register), not merely less common
S6 hedging naturalness: arguably, admittedly, I would argue, might well used where a native speaker would hedge; no stacking of two hedges in one clause
S7 connector truthfulness: pattern.rule describes what the carrier actually does (whereas contrasts, consequently states result, nonetheless concedes-then-holds)
S8 de glosses accurate and idiomatic: trade-off → Abwägung/Kompromiss between two goods, not Handel; drawback → Nachteil; discrepancy → Abweichung; referral → Überweisung; outage → Ausfall
S9 regional neutrality: no US-only institutions the German base cannot gloss; apartment/leasing/parking fine/permit accepted as US-neutral
S10 near-family non-evasion: reviewer confirms each trophy is not a thin synonym or derivation of a forbidden lemma beyond the nearFamilyDecisions already recorded
S11 TTS readability: no abbreviations, no digits, no em dashes, every them turn a complete spoken sentence
S12 no filler: every token in a you turn carries meaning or a taught carrier; no well/basically/you know padding
